reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Characterised by involuntary, large-amplitude, flinging movements affecting the limbs on one side of the body
Classically caused by a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, most often a small vascular event
Movements arise proximally from the shoulder and hip and can be violent enough to cause injury or exhaustion
Hemiballismus and hemichorea form a continuum and frequently coexist in the same patient
In older patients stroke is the leading cause, while non-ketotic hyperglycaemia is an important and reversible cause
Movements characteristically diminish or disappear during sleep
Many vascular cases improve spontaneously over weeks to months
reference.pathophysiology: Hemiballismus results from disruption of the basal ganglia motor circuit, classically through a lesion of the subthalamic nucleus contralateral to the affected side. Loss of the normal excitatory drive from the subthalamic nucleus to the globus pallidus interna reduces inhibitory basal ganglia outflow, thereby disinhibiting thalamocortical projections and releasing the violent, involuntary proximal movements. Vascular lesions are the commonest cause, but any process damaging the subthalamic nucleus or its connections, including metabolic, neoplastic, infective and inflammatory insults, may be responsible.
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to identify a contralateral subthalamic or striatal lesion
Blood glucose and ketones to detect non-ketotic hyperglycaemia
Vascular risk factor assessment and stroke work-up
Screening for neoplastic, structural or inflammatory lesions where imaging is atypical
Metabolic and autoimmune screen in younger patients or atypical presentations
HIV testing where clinically relevant, as it is a recognised cause
redFlags: Movements severe enough to cause self-injury, rhabdomyolysis or exhaustion
Reduced consciousness or additional focal deficits suggesting extensive stroke
Very high blood glucose indicating a hyperglycaemic emergency
Rapid progression suggesting a neoplastic or inflammatory lesion
reference.prognosis: The outlook is often favourable, particularly for vascular hemiballismus, which frequently settles spontaneously over weeks to months; hyperglycaemia-related cases usually improve once glucose is controlled. Symptomatic treatment with dopamine-receptor blocking or VMAT2-modulating agents can reduce disabling movements. Persistent, intractable cases are uncommon and may occasionally warrant consideration of functional neurosurgery.
pitfalls: Failing to check blood glucose, thereby missing reversible non-ketotic hyperglycaemic hemiballismus
Assuming a functional cause and overlooking an underlying stroke
Neglecting measures to prevent injury and exhaustion from violent movements
Overlooking the need for secondary stroke prevention once a vascular cause is confirmed
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Fahn and Jankovic, Principles and Practice of Movement Disorders
management: Treat the underlying cause: correct non-ketotic hyperglycaemia with glycaemic control, which is often reversible, and manage acute stroke with secondary-prevention measures
Suppress the involuntary movements symptomatically with dopamine-receptor-blocking agents such as haloperidol or risperidone, or a VMAT2-modulating agent such as tetrabenazine
Provide supportive care to prevent self-injury and exhaustion, with limb padding and attention to hydration and nutrition during violent movements
Reserve functional neurosurgery such as deep brain stimulation or pallidotomy for severe, disabling and drug-refractory cases
Undertake a vascular risk-factor and stroke work-up, and screen for metabolic, neoplastic, inflammatory and HIV-related causes where imaging is atypical
Refer to neurology and anticipate spontaneous improvement over weeks to months in vascular cases
